job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a recent science exhibition, students explored the hidden world of magnetism. They discovered that magnets are not just simple tools; they are complex objects with specific properties. One experiment showed that when a magnet is heated to a high temperature, it loses its magnetic strength rather than gaining power. Students also tested various materials and found that while iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted to magnets, many other metals like copper and aluminum remain unaffected. This proves that magnetism is a unique force, distinct from static electricity, which involves electric charges. Furthermore, the team observed that a magnet's strength is concentrated at its two ends, known as poles, while the center of the bar magnet shows almost no attraction. To test the nature of magnetic interactions, they brought two magnets together. They saw that like poles repel each other, even if one magnet is much larger than the other. Finally, they learned that a compass needle functions because it aligns with Earth's own magnetic field, not because it is pulled by distant stars. By storing magnets properly with iron keepers, they ensured their magnets would not lose their strength over time, confirming that magnetism is a permanent property, not a temporary energy source that runs out like a battery.

items.evidence: One experiment showed that when a magnet is heated to a high temperature, it loses its magnetic strength rather than gaining power.
items.q: Meena holds a bar magnet in a hot flame for a long time. What happens to it?
options: It becomes much weaker at pulling iron
It becomes stronger from the extra energy
It sticks better, like warm glue
It turns into a static electric charge
items.explain: Heating a magnet to a high temperature makes it lose strength, not gain power.

wrong.why: thinks heat gives a magnet more energy

items.evidence: Students also tested various materials and found that while iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted to magnets, many other metals like copper and aluminum remain unaffected.
items.q: Asha brings a magnet near an aluminium spoon and a nickel coin. What happens?
options: Only the nickel coin is pulled
Both the spoon and the coin are pulled
Neither is pulled, since neither is iron
The coin is pulled only if it is a magnet
items.explain: Nickel is strongly attracted to magnets, but aluminium is a metal that stays unaffected.

items.evidence: This proves that magnetism is a unique force, distinct from static electricity, which involves electric charges.
items.q: How is magnetism different from static electricity?
options: Magnetism is a separate force, not from charges
Magnetism is static electricity under another name
Magnetism is a sticky force, like tape
Magnetism pulls every metal, unlike static electricity
items.explain: Magnetism is its own force; static electricity is the one that involves electric charges.

wrong.why: thinks magnetism and static electricity are the same
thinks magnets work like glue or tape

items.evidence: Furthermore, the team observed that a magnet's strength is concentrated at its two ends, known as poles, while the center of the bar magnet shows almost no attraction.
items.q: Kabir touches the middle of a bar magnet to a paper clip. What happens?
options: The clip is barely attracted at all
The clip is pulled most strongly there
The clip is pulled as much as at the ends
The clip sticks there like on tape
items.explain: A magnet's strength is at its two poles; the centre shows almost no attraction.

wrong.why: thinks the centre is the strongest part
thinks the force is the same everywhere
thinks magnets work like sticky tape

items.evidence: They saw that like poles repel each other, even if one magnet is much larger than the other.
items.q: A big magnet's north pole faces a small magnet's north pole. What happens?
options: The magnets push each other apart
The magnets pull together, as one is bigger
The magnets stick together like glue
The magnets do not affect each other
items.explain: Like poles always repel, even when one magnet is much larger than the other.

wrong.why: thinks a large magnet always attracts a small one
thinks like poles have no effect on each other
